## A New Enforcement Philosophy: Less Trodden Pathways to Better Outcomes

## Keynote Address at the 10th Annual Institute on Corporate &amp; Securities Law in Asia

## Mr Michael Duignan Executive Director, Enforcement

## 24 September 2026

Good morning, everyone. Thank you for having me.

It  is  a  pleasure  to  be  here  for  this  gathering  of  the  region's  corporate  and  securities  law community. Conferences like this give us all a valuable opportunity to compare notes on what is working, and what needs to change.

When I took up the role of Executive Director of Enforcement at the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) late last year one thing that surprised me was the level of interest outside the SFC in my enforcement priorities. Personally, I think it would have been supremely arrogant to take over the Enforcement Division and then immediately say that I knew what it had been doing wrong up to then and what it needed to do differently. In any event, if a case is worth pursuing, we would never reject it simply because it was not on the list of pre-determined priorities. I have never looked at a clearly suspicious insider dealing case and thought we'd better not do it because market manipulation is our stated priority for this year.

Some firms here may disagree, but anybody who suggests that the recent judgements reflect the SFC's current priorities is clearly mistaken. If they tell you anything at all, it will be about the priorities of several years ago. At best.

As time passed, I started to re-frame the question of priorities as a question of my regulatory philosophy.  Put  simply:  we  should  pursue  any  lawful,  workable  approach  that  gets  good outcomes fast and efficiently.

Note: This is the text of the speech as drafted, which may differ from the delivered version.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Philosophies are easy to state but hard to live up to. Anyone can say enforcement should be faster and smarter. The real test is whether it holds up in the midst of a complex case, with incomplete facts, competing priorities, and a clock that doesn't stop ticking. So let me show you how such a philosophy can actually play out in real life.

## The Philosophy: Acting Before the Case Even Begins

Before going into the specifics, let me be clear on one point: enforcement action can be a blunt tool. Sometimes the smartest and fastest enforcement action is the one we never have to take because we have already told the market what not to do.

## Circular to Licensed Corporations Carrying Out Sponsor Work

Take  the  SFC's  circular  published  in  January  aimed  at  licensed  corporations  carrying  out sponsor work, for example 1 .

2025 was a robust year for Hong Kong IPOs. Proceeds rose more than 200% year-on-year 2 , with Hong Kong back at the top of the global listing table. But when volume spikes at such pace, quality has a habit of quietly slipping out the back door.

In the circular, we clearly set out our concerns about what we'd seen and our expectations of sponsors: What we didn't like were listing documents that read like a checklist exercise rather than the product of genuine due diligence; principals stretched across far more live deals than any person could reasonably manage; and, in some cases, sign-offs from people not qualified to do so.

We did not stop at just describing the problem. We went further and drew a bright line. Any principal supervising six or more live deals at once earns a label we do not hand out lightly: a 'Strained Principal.' Firms had one week to flag unqualified staff on live deals, and two weeks to report their full principal-to-deal ratios.

Firms flagged as 'concerning' had three months to complete an internal review and submit a rectification  plan,  signed  off  by  their  Manager-in-Charge.  Separately,  we  raised  the  bar  on competency itself, tightening the licensing exam required before anyone can take on sponsor work at all.

1 Circular to licensed corporations carrying out sponsor work dated 30 January 2026.

2 SFC's Annual Report 2025-26 for the year ended 31 March 2026.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

So why go into so much detail in a circular, rather than waiting for problems to surface case by case?  Because this  is  exactly  the  'fast  and  efficient'  philosophy  I  mentioned,  just  applied upstream.

Our  review  of  live  deals  told  us  that  overstretched  principals  and  thin  diligence  generally produced weak listing  documents,  and  issuers with  weak  listing  documents  often  become enforcement cases in time.

Waiting for that cycle to run its course before acting is neither fast nor efficient. It is slower and less fair to the market because real harm may already be done by the time we act. That is the whole logic of a circular: fix the structural drivers of misconduct - capacity, competency, and incentives - before they produce a case at all. And put the expectations in writing well in advance, so that nobody is surprised when we do take action. We are simply enforcing what we have already said we would.

## Resolving Persistent Intermediary Misconduct: A Case Example

Let me turn to a case example. I can speak only in general terms as the case is not yet public.

Picture a small, local brokerage with serious structural weaknesses. Client monies were not properly  segregated.  Statements  of  account  were  not  reliable.  There  was  no  meaningful separation  of  duties,  no  real  safeguard  against  conflicts  of  interest,  and  no  supervision  of discretionary trading accounts- the sole proprietor was trading for themselves as well as the firm's clients. This was clearly not a firm with one isolated weakness. Although no tangible harm had been caused to the  clients  (yet),  this  was  also  clearly  a  firm  with  little  hope  of improving its operations to an acceptable standard.

Here is how it played out in the end:

- Our Intermediaries Division detected these issues during a routine inspection. They issued a management letter setting out the deficiencies, followed by a letter of mindedness, then hard licensing conditions.
- In parallel, Enforcement also launched a full investigation into the firm's conduct, and the fitness  and  properness  of  its  senior  management, which  confirmed  the  internal  control deficiencies observed by the Intermediaries Division were continuing.
- Our disciplinary team proposed a public reprimand, a significant fine, and a suspension of the Responsible Officer's licence.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

- But disciplinary sanctions would not solve the firm's persistent control deficiencies. So, with the disciplinary proceedings hanging over their heads, we explored whether the firm and its responsible officer and sole shareholder, who was basically managing the firm singlehandedly, might voluntarily surrender their licences instead of proceeding through the full disciplinary process, with Intermediaries Division then supervising an orderly wind-down of the business.

Why does this matter? The conventional route would have meant grinding through potentially months  or  even  years  of  proceedings,  appeals  and  hearings,  to  arrive  eventually  at  a punishment for a firm that probably needed to stop operating some time before.

Enforcement action is  sometimes  taken  in  order  to  send  a  message  to  the  market.  But  a question worth asking at this point is: what would be the best outcome in this situation? We wanted  this  firm  to  stop  operating.  Protecting  the  market  from  a  firm  like  this  is  a  key consideration in deciding how we should exercise our regulatory discretion in this case.

The real threat of enforcement action, together with the hard licensing conditions that were already in place, brought home to the firm that it was best for it to voluntarily agree to stop operating.

That  is  not  a  lesser  outcome  because  it  skipped  the  theatre  of  a  full  hearing.  That  is enforcement working the way it is supposed to: cross-divisional, multi-angled, and focused on the result, not the ritual.

## Serving Minority Shareholders: Two Cases

Let us move from intermediaries to corporate misconduct, and specifically, the interests of minority shareholders, who are so often the last people anyone thinks about until it is far too late.

## PricewaterhouseCoopers Hong Kong

Many  of  you  will  already  be  familiar  with  this  case.  China  Evergrande  Group  (China Evergrande) was, at its peak, one of the largest property developers in the Chinese Mainland, until  it  collapsed  under  a  mountain  of  debt,  defaulted,  and  took  a  great  many  minority shareholders' savings down with it.

Our findings showed that the company had overstated its revenue for years prior to its eventual demise. The case came to our attention not because of the collapse itself, but because of what

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

came before it: financial accounts that, on the whole, gave investors the impression matters were less dire than feared - until they proved otherwise.

The settlement I want to discuss concerns PricewaterhouseCoopers Hong Kong (PwC HK), China Evergrande's auditor 3 . The matter is currently the subject of judicial review proceedings, so I shall confine my remarks to public information. Now, the obvious question is: why pursue the auditor when it was apparently the company that falsified its own books? In the SFC's view, the auditor had failed in a number of respects:

- It failed to maintain auditor independence during the audits of China Evergrande's financial statements for the fiscal years 2019 and 2020;
- It failed to exercise adequate professional scepticism in audit planning, in carrying out audit procedures, and in handling audit irregularities;
- It failed to design and perform effective site inspections to ascertain the construction and delivery status of properties for proper revenue recognition;
- More  troubling  still,  it  actively  acquiesced  to  manipulation  by  China  Evergrande's management of audit samples and site inspections which facilitated the concealment of premature revenue recognition; and
- Finally,  it  failed  to  sufficiently  verify  the  authenticity  of  the  supporting  documents  and records.

Taken together, these failures matter because auditors sit at the centre of market trust - they are  the  independent  check  investors  rely  on  when  they  cannot  verify  a  company's  books themselves,  and  when  that  check  fails,  the  harm  falls  squarely  on  independent  minority shareholders who had no way of knowing better.

We could have pursued proceedings before the Market Misconduct Tribunal, or through the courts,  seeking  compensation  down  a  long  and  uncertain  road.  Or  we  could  consider  a settlement  with  the  auditor  directly,  and  secure  immediate  redress  for  those  affected  independent minority shareholders.

We chose the latter path. PwC HK agreed to pay $1 billion to compensate independent minority shareholders as part of a package of remedial measures, without admitting liability. The SFC

3 See SFC press release dated 23 April 2026 on the settlement with PwC HK.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

will take no further action against PwC HK on the basis that PwC HK fulfils the terms of the settlement agreement.

This  approach,  novel  at  least  for  Hong  Kong,  has  since  been  challenged  in  court.  The liquidators of China Evergrande have argued that the SFC lacked the power to enter into this kind of out of court settlement, and that doing so disturbed the ordinary priority of claims in a liquidation.

Our position, as we put to the court in August, is that this settlement was a voluntary agreement with PwC HK, entered into under our general contracting powers, and that the court-supervised process  under  section  213  of  the  Securities  and  Futures  Ordinance  only  applies  once  we actually commence proceedings under it, which we did not do here. The settlement does not disturb the priority of claims among China Evergrande's creditors, because the $1 billion in question belongs to PwC HK, not to China Evergrande's estate, and was never part of the assets available to satisfy claims against the company.

On that basis, the arrangement sits outside the liquidation process, and the statutory priority of distribution the liquidators say was bypassed was never actually engaged. Those arguments are now before the Court. Judgment is expected around the end of October.

What this  also  illustrates  is  a  broader  point:  any  new  approach,  however  well-intentioned, carries an element of risk. That risk is a real factor to weigh, but it is not the only one. No regulatory decision is ever universally welcomed, but the key question is whether the public interest is best served by the course being taken.

One further point, for those of you advising licensed corporations: some have asked whether a licensed corporation could settle a disciplinary matter without accepting liability, on the same basis as PwC HK. The answer is no , and the reason is structural. When we bring disciplinary proceedings against a licensed corporation, we have already made a determination that a breach occurred.

In a sense, we are the standard-setter and the decision-maker in that process, which is one of the reasons why there has to be an external appeal body to hear the facts afresh. Litigation against  a  third  party  like  an  auditor  is  a  different  exercise  entirely,  and  a  no-admission settlement there allows us to secure compensation for investors faster than years of contested proceedings would have allowed. Whether no-admission is appropriate will always depend on the facts of the case, the evidence, and practical considerations on both sides. That was the

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

calculus for PwC HK, one that does not carry over to our own disciplinary framework, where a breach has already been found.

## Giordano International Limited

Let me give you one more example from the takeovers context. This was not a case handled by  the  Enforcement  Division,  but  I  signed  the  agreement  as  my  last  act  as  head  of  the Corporate Finance Division.

Under  the  Code  on  Takeovers  and  Mergers  (Takeovers  Code),  there  is  a  simple  but fundamental principle: when a person, together with parties acting in concert, crosses 30% of a listed company's voting rights, a mandatory offer follows. This gives every other shareholder the same opportunity to exit as the new controlling group has effectively given itself. It is not just a technical rule-it protects minority shareholders when control is acquired or consolidated.

The  company  involved  here  was  Giordano  International  Limited  (Giordano),  a  well-known Hong Kong fashion retailer 4 .

The names behind the case would also be familiar to many in this region: the relevant vehicles sat within the Chow Tai Fook Nominee Limited group, associated with the Cheng family, one of Hong Kong's best-known business families.

According to public disclosures, the group had held shares in Giordano through Sino Wealth International Limited since 2011, but its disclosed shareholding had consistently stayed below 30%.

The problem was what the market could not see. In the public disclosures, the Chow Tai Fook Nominee Limited group appeared to remain below 30%.

But after investigating Giordano's shareholding structure, the Takeovers Executive considered that two other shareholders, Best Sincere Limited and Firstrate Enterprises Limited, had been acting in concert with the group.

Once those holdings were counted, two things followed. First, the 30% threshold had been crossed  in  May  2016,  requiring  a  mandatory  offer  at  $3.60  per  share.  Second,  the  2022 voluntary  offer  at  $1.88  per  share  should  have  become  unconditional,  rather  than  being allowed to lapse.

4 See SFC press release dated 16 February 2026 on the settlement relating to Giordano.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

This  was  not  simply  a  paperwork  failure.  The  alleged  non-disclosure  of  the  concert  party relationship went to the heart of two core protections under the Takeovers Code: first, the right of  shareholders  to  receive  a  mandatory  offer  once  control  crosses  30%;  and  second,  the assurance that, once an offer is announced, it must proceed unless a stated condition has genuinely failed. These rules go to the integrity of the takeover regime itself, without which shareholders could not trust that control changes are disclosed or that offers will be honoured.

Under normal circumstances, such a breach might be addressed by requiring a fresh takeover offer. But here, the alleged breaches occurred too long ago for that to be a sensible remedy. An offer to the current shareholders would have rewarded an entirely different group from those affected by the apparent breaches of the Code.

The settlement outcome was therefore significant. It required cash payments to independent shareholders who held Giordano shares on the relevant breach dates.

It  is  always  difficult  to  be  precise  about  which  shareholders  will  ultimately  receive  what compensation, but the maximum total payment could reach as much as $1.5 billion.

This is also where the case fits the broader theme of today's remarks. We could have taken the matter through a contested hearing before the Takeovers and Mergers Panel. That route remains important, and in some cases it is necessary.

But it would also have involved time, cost, and uncertainty. Here, the Takeovers Executive weighed those factors and concluded that settlement best served the interest of the investing public. One might argue this was, in some sense, rough justice - but attempting to rewrite history is always going to be an imprecise exercise.

This  is  the  same  pragmatic  instinct  behind  the  PwC  HK  outcome:  where  the  regulatory objective is clear, and where investor redress can be achieved sooner, a carefully structured settlement can deliver more for investors than a longer fight ever would.

And  if  you  are  wondering  why  I  have  walked  you  through  these  examples  together,  it  is because they are not really separate stories.

Together with the sponsor circular, they represent the same philosophy in different forms: a circular that tells the market what not to do, a voluntary licence surrender instead of a drawnout disciplinary process, a settlement instead of years in a tribunal or court. The tools differ,

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

but the logic underneath is the same - give people fair notice, then act decisively and efficiently once the moment calls for it.

## Suspending Trading: Acting Before Harm Compounds

Let me address one more tool directly: our power, under the Securities and Futures (Stock Market Listing) Rules (SMLR), to direct the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited to suspend trading in a listed company's shares.

This is not a specific Enforcement power, but it often arises as a result of investigations carried out by the Enforcement Division. Generally we would prefer that shareholders and investors have the opportunity to trade.

So we recognise that a suspension of trading is a significant step. It limits shareholders' ability to  trade  and,  particularly  where  a  suspension  is  prolonged,  can  have  serious  practical consequences for investors. These effects should not be understated. That is precisely why the decision must be considered carefully in light of the circumstances of each case.

Some commentators make the point that retail shareholders can be 'trapped' when trading is suspended.  Of  course  this  would  be  equally  true  when  the  trading  is  suspended  by  the Exchange or by the Company, which is much more frequently the case. But let's stick with suspensions  directed  by  the  SFC  for  now,  as  these  mostly  arise  due  to  concerns  about inaccurate, misleading - whether by omission or commission - or downright false statements.

My main point is that the commentators rarely go on to ask the harder questions: if the market is  not  a  properly  informed  market  and  trading  continued  as  normal,  who  would  these shareholders actually be selling to?

And at  what  price,  when  the  very  information  needed  to  price  those  shares  properly  is  in serious doubt? There are no easy answers to those questions.

Allowing  trading  to  continue  does  not  solve  the  problem;  it  simply  transfers  it  to  the  next unsuspecting buyer. The suspension itself does not undo the loss that has already occurred. But it is often the first step towards a genuine remedy. In many cases, we go on to take action through the courts to require those responsible for the misconduct to buy back the shares at an appropriate price.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

It  may  be  an  imperfect  and  delayed  solution.  But  it  seems  preferable  to  the  alternative  of allowing other, unsuspecting retail investors to buy those same shares, while we already have serious concerns about the company's true financial position.

The purpose behind a suspension is not to punish the company or its shareholders. It is a protective measure intended to preserve an orderly and informed market where the available information may no longer provide a reliable basis for trading.

We must consider the interests of not only those shareholders who wish to sell, but also those who continue to hold the shares and those who may buy without knowing the full picture.

These are not always easy calls. The choice is rarely between an option that causes harm and one  that  does  not.  The  question  is  whether,  in  the  particular  circumstances  and  on  the information available, the risks of continued trading outweigh the consequences of temporarily restricting it.

It can however be regarded as a blunt tool for dealing with information deficits. That was one reason for proposing changes to the SMLR in our consultation paper published in March 2025. The proposals included the ability to impose conditions, as an alternative to suspension of trading. We expect such conditions will often involve additional disclosures. These proposals have received broad support and constructive feedback, which is all being taken into account as  part  of  the  drafting  process  for  the  necessary  legislative  amendments. That  process  is ongoing.

All of which brings me to the final thoughts I would like to leave with you.

## Closing: Going the Less Trodden Path

None of what I have described today is an argument against process. It is an argument against treating one particular process as the only legitimate route to a good outcome, regardless of the specific needs of the case.

The conventional route will always matter - investigation, notice, hearing, tribunal. But it is not the only way through, and defaulting to it in every case carries its own cost: slower outcomes, delayed redress, and sometimes leaving real harm unaddressed longer than necessary.

Sometimes, the faster, and frankly better, route is the settlement, the early circular,  or the voluntary resolution that fixes a problem before it becomes a multi-year set of proceedings.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

I hope that those of you in the room advising people who find themselves on the other side of the  desk  from  the  SFC,  can  agree  with  that  premise. And  I  look  forward  to  constructive discussions designed to achieve that more effective outcome. A more collaborative approach should achieve a better outcome for those affected by the identified misconduct.

It will also release resources for the SFC to focus on the very worst actors, who do nothing to improve the reputation of the Hong Kong market, who cause untold misery to many and as a direct  result  of  their  actions  increases  the  costs  for  everyone  in  this  room.  Surely  every rightminded person would want us to be focussed on such cheats.

I hope you found my ramblings of at least some interest and I am sure that there will be much more of interest over the next two days. Thank you very much for your attention.
